A flaw is an imperfection — something that is wrong with, or missing from, a person or thing, which prevents it from being as good, strong, or perfect as it should be.

Think of it this way: imagine something ideal — a perfect diamond, a perfect plan, a perfect person. Now imagine that same thing, but with one thing wrong with it. That "one thing wrong" is the flaw.

A flaw is almost always undesirable. It reduces quality, weakens something, or makes something fail to meet the standard it was supposed to meet.
The Three Main Ways "Flaw" Is Used

1. A Physical Flaw (in an object)

This is a crack, scratch, chip, blemish, or any physical defect in an object — something you can often see or feel.

Examples:

  • "The jeweler examined the diamond carefully and found a tiny flaw inside it."
  • "This vase is being sold cheaply because of a flaw on its surface."
  • "The engineer discovered a flaw in the metal beam that could cause the bridge to collapse."

Notice that a flaw in an object often makes it less valuable, less beautiful, or structurally weaker. Importantly, a flaw is usually an inherent defect — meaning it exists within the object itself, not just surface-level damage caused later. A scratch from dropping a glass is damage. A bubble trapped inside the glass during its making is a flaw.

2. A Logical or Structural Flaw (in a plan, argument, system, or idea)

When something non-physical — like a plan, a theory, a law, a process, or an argument — has a mistake, weakness, or gap in it that makes it incorrect or likely to fail, that weakness is called a flaw.

Examples:

  • "The lawyer found a flaw in the contract that made it legally invalid."
  • "Your argument sounds convincing, but there is a flaw in your reasoning — you assumed something that isn't true."
  • "The plan seemed brilliant, but it had one major flaw: it didn't account for bad weather."
  • "Scientists found a flaw in the original study, which meant its results could not be trusted."

In this sense, a flaw is essentially a point of failure — the weak link in the chain, or the hole in the logic, that undermines the whole thing.

3. A Character Flaw (in a person)

A person can also have flaws — not physical ones, but weaknesses in their personality, character, or behaviour. These are habits, tendencies, or traits that hold a person back, hurt others, or prevent them from being the best version of themselves.

Examples:

  • "He is generous and kind, but his greatest flaw is his inability to control his anger."
  • "She is very talented, but her flaw is that she is too proud to ask for help."
  • "Jealousy was his fatal flaw — it destroyed every good relationship he had."

Character flaws make people human and realistic in stories and in life. Nobody is without them. A flaw doesn't make a person entirely bad — it just means there is something they struggle with or need to improve.

A flaw is not always visible at first. Flaws are often hidden beneath the surface. A diamond may look perfect to the eye but have a flaw only an expert can detect. A plan may sound brilliant in a meeting but have a flaw that only becomes obvious when it fails. This is what makes flaws particularly dangerous — you may not notice them until it is too late.

A flaw is not the same as total failure. Something can have a flaw and still function, still be beautiful, still be useful. A flawed diamond is still a diamond. A flawed person can still be a good person. A flaw just means something is less than perfect — it does not mean something is worthless.

Flaws vary in severity. A flaw can be minor (a tiny scratch on a watch) or catastrophic (a crack in an airplane wing). This is why English speakers often describe the degree of a flaw:

  • a minor flaw / a small flaw — not very serious
  • a serious flaw / a significant flaw — quite important
  • a major flaw / a critical flaw — very serious, hard to ignore
  • a fatal flaw — so serious that it causes total failure or destruction (see below)

A fatal flaw is a flaw so serious and so fundamental that it causes the complete failure, destruction, or downfall of something or someone. The word "fatal" here doesn't always mean "deadly" — it means "causing complete failure."

Examples:

  • "The product had a fatal flaw in its design — it overheated and had to be recalled."
  • "His fatal flaw was his arrogance — he always believed he was the smartest person in the room, and it cost him everything."
  • "The prosecution's case had a fatal flaw: the key witness was unreliable."

In literature and storytelling, a fatal flaw (sometimes called hamartia) is a classic concept — it is the one weakness in an otherwise great or powerful character that leads to their downfall. Think of a brilliant king who is too proud to listen to advice. That pride is his fatal flaw.

The adjective flawless means having absolutely no flaws — perfectly made, perfectly executed, perfectly beautiful. It is a high compliment.

  • "The diamond was flawless."
  • "Her performance was absolutely flawless."
  • "He delivered the speech flawlessly."

——

A flaw is a defect, weakness, or imperfection in something or someone that makes it less than it should be. It can exist in a physical object (a crack in glass), in an idea or plan (a hole in the logic), or in a person's character (a tendency toward dishonesty). Flaws range from minor to fatal. They are often hidden. Having a flaw doesn't mean something is worthless, but a fatal flaw can cause total failure. The opposite of flawed is flawless — meaning perfect, with nothing wrong.
